foodDescription: Dense, dark, slightly sour rye bread, served with almost every meal. Estonians abroad say it is what they miss most.
Rye bread topped with butter, spiced Baltic sprats, boiled egg, and herbs. A classic snack, often with a shot of vodka or a beer.
Sausage of blood and barley, baked until crisp and served with lingonberry jam. A Christmas tradition, eaten all winter.
Mashed potatoes and barley topped with fried bacon and onions. Country food from southern Estonia, now on restaurant menus as comfort food.
Pork set in its own jelly, cut cold and eaten with mustard or vinegar. Usually on the table at Christmas.
A pink salad of beets, potatoes, pickles, herring, and sour cream. Common at parties and holidays.
A thick, salty, sour soup of mixed meats, pickles, olives, and lemon, served with sour cream. Brought from Russia and loved here.
A mix of roasted barley, rye, oat, and pea flour, stirred into buttermilk or kefir. A uniquely Estonian food, eaten for breakfast or in desserts.
A small bar of sweet curd cheese coated in chocolate, sold in every supermarket fridge. A childhood favorite.
Tallinn claims to have invented marzipan in the Town Hall Pharmacy. Whatever the truth, the city has been selling it for centuries, and you can watch figures being painted at the Kalev marzipan room.
A dark, sweet rum-based liqueur with vanilla and citrus, made since 1960. Drunk neat, in coffee, or poured over ice cream.
Estonia drinks a lot of beer. Saku and A. Le Coq are the big brands, and Tallinn has a lively craft brewing scene, especially around Telliskivi.
